title: From the Coast to Ayacucho: Crossing the Spine of the Andes – Ryan Wilson
content:
After a multi-year trip across Asia, Ryan Wilson returns to the Andes Mountains to link up new routes he’s had his sights set on for years.  Follow along as he climbs from Peru’s rugged desert coast to the high Andes and to Ayacucho…

If you’ve spent much time perusing The Radavist over the last decade, you know by now that I’m a huge fan of the riding in the Andes. At this point, it feels kind of like a home away from home. There are few places on earth that have this combination of dramatic landscapes mixed with quiet roads, fascinating culture, and incredible camping opportunities.

Every few years, I’ll find myself scrolling over near South America on the map toward some of the countless routes that I’ve mapped out here over the years, but have yet to ride, and my mind starts to formulate how I could link them up to form a new route.

After a few years in Asia, where it’s very rare that I can speak much of the local language of the country I’m in, it’s also a nice break from relying on Google Translate for everything, and it’s great to be able to strike up a conversation with just about anyone, even if my Español got a little rusty while I was away.

Starting from the Bottom

The zone from central Peru, down toward Northern Patagonia, is about as good as it gets for bike travel, as you can link up thousands of kilometers of quiet, scenic roads virtually the entire way. This would be the stretch of South America that I’d focus on for this trip, starting in a coastal city just south of Lima, Peru, called Chincha Alta.

I would forgo the classic Peru Divide on this trip and instead link up some of the bustling Spanish colonial cities that are tucked into the high Andes. But first, as any good Peru trip starts, I had to ascend all the way up from that desert coastline to well over 16,000ft in one big steady climb.

This could seem like some form of torture to start a trip with 3 days of nonstop uphill, but these are some of my favorite parts of Peru. You get to ride through many different zones, from the first barren folds of the Andes, as cacti and trees slowly fill the valleys, on the way to the more fertile zones up around 10,000ft, and then up into the frigid, windswept highlands where there are more llamas than people.

The Desert Coast

I left the chaotic streets of Chincha Alta on the day of the weekly street market, with my bags full of any supplies I might need for the next 2-3 days. There would be some settlements along the way, but I didn’t really have an idea about what I might find in local shops. Sometimes it’s as barren as Coke and some various cookies.

The area right near the coast is reasonably cool, but as you make your way into the lower Andes, that sea breeze disappears, and the equatorial sun begins to cook. I was thankful that some of the first settlements had small tiendas with big water bottles stuffed into frigid coolers, something of a rarity in Peru.

These parts of the country are also home to many petroglyphs, some of which are up to 4,000 years old, like at Petroglifos de Huancor, where around 200 engraved rocks can be found, only a short walk from the road.

The broken pavement road continued gradually up the valley until I spotted some trees down by the river shortly after sunset. It was just far enough away from the road that I decided to set up camp. At this altitude, it would be one of the only mild camping nights of my entire time in Peru. Oftentimes, you have to sprint into your sleeping bag and close up the tent right when the sun goes down in the Peruvian Andes, so I tried to savor this one.

The Temperate Zone

By the time I reached roughly 10,000 feet of altitude the next day, there were more farms and villages popping up across the hillsides. When asked where I was going, people were constantly confused as I said Ayacucho. They would insist that I’d gone the wrong way and should turn around, go all the way back to Chincha, and take another valley that was further to the south. I would reassure them that I took this road to avoid that traffic, but to them it made more sense for me to descend back 10,000 ft of elevation and re-climb all of that along a main road, I guess to avoid some dirt roads in the high mountains. “Me gustan las trochas” (I like the dirt roads), I’d say with a smile as they squeeze my tires.

I spent a day in a small accommodation in Villa de Arma to help with my acclimatization a bit. It wasn’t much, but it would have to get me through the next stretch, which would find me climbing well over 16,000 ft and camping at very high altitudes.

Into the Puna

For a (mostly) paved road, I was shocked by how little traffic there was. On the slow and steady climb up to the high puna, I don’t recall seeing more than a couple of vehicles. Most of the company I shared on my way up was in the form of alpacas, roaming around, chomping on vegetation, and looking on with skepticism as I rode by.

At one of the first high points on the route, a view to the north opened up, with my first sight of snow-covered mountains in the distance. Shortly after, I came across a flat spot tucked next to a small lake and a ridgeline at 4650m or 15,256ft and decided to set up camp. I knew it was going to be a long night at this altitude. The cold is one thing, but the main issue is trying to sleep properly without proper acclimatization, which makes it very challenging to fall asleep and stay asleep, despite being pretty well spent from the climb. I’d get used to the lack of air pretty soon, though, because the next few days would all be spent at these lofty heights.

Off the Beaten Track

The morning brought sweet relief from the cold, but the sun didn’t last long. By the time I was packed up, the clouds were already moving in. I had some ups and downs across the desolate landscape before I turned off the “main road”, if you want to call it that, and headed for a shortcut through a canyon.

Frigid rain began to trickle down as I descended into the canyon. Slowly, the road was looking less and less used as I passed through a small, seemingly deserted mining area. I came up to an open gate, with no one around, but I wasn’t going to wait for somebody to come along and tell me to turn around, so I kept heading downhill.

With every bend, I was becoming more skeptical that this road would even connect to where I was trying to go. It was heading down into some very rugged terrain, and I struggled to spot a recent-looking tire track on the road’s surface. But I was committed now, having descended far too much to consider turning back.

Thankfully, the track squeezed through the narrow canyon and came out the other side to a pristine dirt road. Just a couple of kilometers further, I came across a few shepherds who waved me down, telling me in a serious tone that this was a private mining access road, despite the lack of signage. They assumed I took a wrong turn, but when I told them the name of the village I was trying to get to, about 25km down the road, their concern level dropped, and they sent me on my way with some info about the route.

In the clear now, after going through the exit gate, I climbed up from the low point a bit and scrambled up a hillside toward a hidden-from-the-road flat spot and called it a night.

Over the Top

The first real village I’d seen in a couple of days was Santa Ana. Of course it was a Sunday, so the place was deserted, and the only restaurant in town was closed. But I was fortunate enough to meet a local man who must have felt bad when I nearly shed a tear as he told me about the restaurant, because he went to his home and tracked me down with some freshly boiled potatoes and an avocado, which really complemented the saltine crackers and cookies that I found at the small shop well.

There was one more climb left to tackle before I’d be on the biggest descent of the trip so far. But first, I’d have to make it to over 4960m / 16,273ft.

The road gradually twisted and turned its way up another mountain. Ominous clouds gathered nearby, with light painting the mountainsides. It was looking pretty iffy as I summited the pass, but thankfully I was heading the opposite direction with nearly 60 kilometers of descent in front of me before I’d reach the town of Lircay, the biggest I’d seen since leaving Chincha Alta.

It was the perfect spot to rest up for a couple of days and catch the local festivities where locals dress up in traditional costumes and whip each other with ropes.

The Road to the Big City

From Lircay, I had a shade over two days of riding to get to Ayacucho. I mapped a route over the most remote road I could find, and immediately found myself sheltering in a small village when a rare thunder-snowstorm hit. It started with lightning and hail, but gradually morphed into full-on snow as I hid under a small metal roof next to a house. A local man joined me who was riding up the road on a motorcycle.

I ended up waiting it out for around an hour and a half before getting back on the road just as the sun broke through the clouds for the last bit of light of the day. Needless to say, it was a very frosty night in the tent.

A roller coaster of ups and downs led me straight toward one of my favorite cities in Peru, Ayacucho. It happens to also be one of the very few places where you can reliably get one of my favorite meals in Peru, the Puca Picante. It’s a dish with a vibrant red sauce made primarily from blended beets and peanuts to go with the usual Andean staples of rice, potatoes, red onions, and crispy pork. It’s local to this region, so when I rolled into the city around lunchtime, I searched around all of the almuerzo spots to track one down. It was a perfect way to cap off my first couple of weeks back in the Andes.
